page.title: Help
page.subtitle: Everything you need to use Nebulis, from first install to everyday use.

whatIsNebulis.title: What is Nebulis
whatIsNebulis.lead: Your astrophotography library and session planner, running on your own machine.
whatIsNebulis.p1: Connect a smart telescope and Nebulis pulls in every session automatically, building one library sorted by object and by night, with full capture history, FITS metadata, and your own notes attached. Check the Forecast before you head out for a single sky score built from cloud cover, seeing, and moon phase. Use Explore to find something worth photographing, then the Planner to turn your list into a real schedule for the hours you have.
whatIsNebulis.p2: It doesn't edit, stack, or control your telescope. Those jobs already have tools built for them. Nebulis is what happens after: everything your gear captured, organized into something you can use. It also scores your raw frames, tracks how much time each object has left, and builds a ZIP of your best frames, with matching calibration frames, for PixInsight or Siril.
whatIsNebulis.runsLocally: Runs entirely on your own computer. Every image stays on hardware you own, for as long as you want it.

quickAnswers.title: Quick answers
quickAnswers.subtitle: The things most people want to know first.

sendImages.q: Does Nebulis send my images anywhere?
sendImages.a: No. Nebulis runs on your own machine and your images stay there. Nothing leaves your network unless you choose to share it.

whichTelescopes.a: ZWO SeeStar S30, S30 Pro, S50, and S50 Pro, the ZWO ASIAIR, and DWARFLAB Dwarf 3, Dwarf II, and Dwarf Mini. There is also a generic option for any SMB share that follows the same folder layout, such as a NAS or another camera.

firstSteps.q: I just installed it. What do I do first?
firstSteps.a: Create your account, add a telescope under Settings → Telescopes, set your location under Settings → Sky, then run an import. That is the whole setup.

newImages.q: How do new images get into my library?
newImages.a: Sync from the telescope icon in the top bar, or turn on auto-import in Settings → Telescopes. You can also import files you already have from a folder.

viewOnPhone.q: Can I view my library on a phone or TV?
viewOnPhone.a: Yes. Nebulis has iOS, Apple TV, and Android apps that connect to your server over the same network. Pair them under Settings → Account → Devices.

objectFilters.q: What does each object filter include?
objectFilters.a: Filters group objects by their catalog type, matching the type text itself. Those type names come from the catalog and stay in English whatever language you use, so the words that matter are "galaxy", "nebula" and "cluster". Any type containing "galaxy" lands in the galaxy filter: spiral, barred, irregular, lenticular and starburst galaxies, plus galaxy groups, pairs and triplets. "nebula" covers emission, reflection, dark and planetary nebulae, and supernova remnants count as nebulae too. "cluster" covers open and globular clusters. An object can appear under more than one filter: a planetary nebula is both a nebula and a planetary nebula, a supernova remnant is both a nebula and a supernova remnant, and Cluster + Nebula is both a cluster and a nebula. Where a count has to choose one family, Cluster + Nebula counts as a nebula, because the nebulosity is what it is imaged for. The Library adds finer filters on top: solar system objects, comets, stars, planetary nebulae, supernova remnants, and Unknown, which holds objects whose type could not be resolved.

findTarget.q: How do I find something to photograph?
findTarget.a: Open Explore in the top menu. Search any name or catalog number, or browse by kind: galaxies, emission nebulae, planetary nebulae, supernova remnants, star clusters and showpieces. Each object says whether you can see it from your site tonight and whether it fits your telescope's frame. From there you can add it to your wishlist or plan it for tonight.

bestTonight.a: It is the same score in the Planner, Explore and Wishlist. It blends how well a target is placed tonight (how high it climbs and for how long) with how rewarding it is to shoot. The Planner's Order menu also offers Best conditions.

classicPage.q: Can I get the old object page back?
classicPage.a: Yes. Use the small toggle at the top right of any object page to switch between the Combined page and the Classic page, a grid of observations. To change the default, go to Settings → Library → Object pages. Classic may be removed in a future version.

badFrames.q: How do I find and remove bad frames?
badFrames.a: Open a night's observation page and look at its Sub-frames list. Every raw frame has a score from 0 to 100 and a Good, Fair or Bad grade against the rest of its night. Select the bad ones and discard them, or mark frames Keep or Reject so they are left out when you export for stacking. See Frame quality and stacking.

locationSharing.q: Does Nebulis send my location anywhere?
locationSharing.a: Only to fetch conditions for your sky. Your observing site's coordinates go to Open-Meteo and 7Timer for the forecast, and to DarkSkySites for your light pollution class. Those are the coordinates of the site you set up in Settings, not your device's location, and nothing else about you is included. Every service Nebulis uses is listed under Settings, Data Sources.

gettingStarted.title: Getting started
gettingStarted.lead: You are already signed in, so start with the telescope. Then set where you observe and pull your first night.
gettingStarted.step1Body: Open Settings → Telescopes → Add smart telescope. Press Find device to look for SeeStar, ASIAIR and Dwarf devices on your network, or pick your model and enter the address yourself. The share name and other defaults fill in on their own.
gettingStarted.step1AltA: Settings → Telescopes, with the Add smart telescope button at the bottom of the list
gettingStarted.step1AltB: The Add Smart Telescope dialog, with telescope type, display name, badge color, and connection fields
gettingStarted.step2Body: Settings → Sky → Observing sites. Latitude, longitude, and timezone are required for the Planner, Forecast and Explore to do anything useful. You can add a photo of each site too.
gettingStarted.step2Alt: Settings → Sky, showing an observing site with its name, coordinates, and minimum altitude
gettingStarted.step3Body: Open the telescope icon in the top bar and choose Sync. The first run copies everything, so it is the slowest one. Later runs only move new files.
gettingStarted.step3Alt: The telescope pill in the top bar, open to show each telescope with a Sync button and a Sync all option

tour.title: A tour of the app
tour.lead: Learn what each page does and how to use it.
tour.body: Select a page from the menu on the left to learn what it does, why you'd use it, and how to get the most out of it.

tourLibrary.title: Library
tourLibrary.lead: Your home base. Every object you have imaged shows as a card with its best photo.
tourLibrary.step1Body: Type a catalog ID like M51, a common name like Whirlpool, or a constellation. The toolbar under the search box has a button each for Filters (object type, telescope and status), Favorites, View (group, sort and grid size) and Add (upload files or log a new observation). Active filters show as chips you can remove, and the reset arrow in each menu restores its defaults.
tourLibrary.step1Alt: The Library toolbar with the Filters menu open, listing object types, telescopes and status, and filter chips under the search box
tourLibrary.step2Body: Open View and drag Grid size toward the small grid for up to 10 columns, or toward the large one for as few as 2. From 6 columns the cards switch to a compact layout. The Layout control switches the grid to a Mosaic, where each tile is sized by how much you have done with that object, so your most worked targets stand out. The Gallery has the same Layout control. Nebulis remembers your choice in this browser, and phones stay at 2 columns. Tap any card to open the object page, and star it to mark it as a favorite.
tourLibrary.step2Alt: The Library as a Mosaic, with larger tiles for the objects with the most imaging time
tourLibrary.step3Body: Open an object, tap Notes, and log your personal rating, seeing quality, Bortle class, location, equipment used, and any thoughts about the session. These notes attach to that session permanently so you can reference them anytime.
tourLibrary.step3Alt: The Session Notes dialog filled in with a personal rating, seeing rating, Bortle class, location, equipment, and notes
tourLibrary.step4Body: On an object's page, use the buttons under its name to Add observation or Download all frames as a ZIP. The ... menu holds Plan a night, Compare, Combine subs, Export for stacking and Framing & mosaic. Upload your finished processed image to use it as the thumbnail. Once you have a final stack, delete the raw sub-frames to free up disk space while keeping the stacked result and all metadata.
tourLibrary.step4Alt: An object page's action buttons, with the ... menu open showing Plan a night, Compare, Combine subs and Export for stacking
tourLibrary.step5Body: Go to Settings → Storage to see a full breakdown of which objects are using the most disk space, sorted largest first. This makes it easy to find and manage the heavy ones when you need to free up room.
tourLibrary.step5Alt: The Storage page, showing overall disk usage and a per-object breakdown table sorted by total size

tourObjects.title: Object Details
tourObjects.lead: View all your imaging history for a specific object. Track sessions, metadata, processed images, and visibility forecasts in one place.
tourObjects.step1Body: Click any object in your Library to open its page. The banner shows the object's name, one line with its status and the telescopes you used, its other names, and a single row of figures: observations, sub-frames, magnitude and distance. The star adds it to your favorites. Tonight's visibility and the filter recommendations sit in a panel beside it. About, with the object's type, constellation, coordinates, angular size and description, is a collapsed row at the bottom of the page.
tourObjects.step1Alt: An object page banner with the name, status line, other names, a row of figures, and the Tonight panel beside it
tourObjects.step2Body: The Tonight panel says whether the object is visible from your observing site and when it is best to image. It shows the current altitude, the peak altitude and when it happens, an altitude curve for the night, and the best months of the year to shoot it. The filter recommendations below it suggest which filters suit this object and tonight's Moon.
tourObjects.step2Alt: The Tonight panel with an altitude curve, current altitude, best months and filter recommendations
tourObjects.step3Title: See every picture in one place
tourObjects.step3Body: The Combined page, now the default, gathers everything you have of the object under one set of tabs: All, Subframes, Nights and Projects. Processed, Telescope and Videos tabs appear when you have any. Your processed images show large at the top. Open a picture to see it full size, or open a night to see its sub-frames. Use the toggle at the top right to switch to the Classic page, a grid of observations. You can pick the default under Settings → Library → Object pages. Classic may be removed in a future version.
tourObjects.step3Alt: The Combined object page, with your processed images large at the top and tabs for All, Subframes, Nights and Projects
tourObjects.step4Title: Review your nights and their frames
tourObjects.step4Body: The Nights tab lists every night you imaged this object, newest first, with the telescope, number of sub-frames, cloud cover and temperature. Open a night to see its stacked image, its raw sub-frames and its FITS metadata. The Subframes tab shows how each raw frame measured: see Frame quality and stacking.
tourObjects.step4Alt: The Nights tab, listing each night with its telescope, sub-frame count and weather
tourObjects.step5Body: The Integration card shows the time you have shot through each filter, a goal you can set for each one, and how much is left. Processing Projects share the card, so you can mark an object as Unprocessed, Processing or Processed and keep your Siril or PixInsight project file with it. See Integration and rigs.
tourObjects.step5Alt: The Integration card with a bar for each filter, its goal and the time left, next to the Processing Projects list
tourObjects.step6Body: For each night, you can tap the Notes icon to record your personal experience. Log your seeing rating (1-5 stars), sky darkness (Bortle scale), observing location, equipment used, weather conditions, and any thoughts about the imaging run. These notes stay permanently attached to that night so you can remember what worked well and what to try differently next time.
tourObjects.step6Alt: Session notes form showing star rating, seeing, Bortle, location, and equipment fields
tourObjects.note: All session notes, metadata, and observations stay permanently attached to their object. Revisit any object years later and you'll still have exactly what you captured, what equipment you used, and your thoughts from that observing session.

tourGallery.title: Gallery
tourGallery.lead: Every frame from your library in one grid, with a filter to narrow it down to just your finished results.
tourGallery.step1Title: Browse every frame, or just the processed ones
tourGallery.step1Body: The header shows totals for images, objects, processed finals, and favorites. By default the grid includes every frame in your library; turn on Processed only to see just the JPG, PNG, and TIFF finals you've uploaded. Search by object name, filter by object type, or sort the grid to find what you're after. The Layout control switches the grid to a Mosaic that sizes each tile by how much you have done with that object.
tourGallery.step1Alt: Image Gallery page showing header stats and a grid of thumbnails, with Favorites, Processed only, and object-type filters
tourGallery.step2Body: Click any thumbnail to open it in a full-screen viewer. Toggle between Fit and 1:1 to zoom in on detail, favorite or share the image, and download it. Tap the target button to Annotate the picture with rings and names for the objects in it. On a raw frame, press K to keep it or X to reject it. A filmstrip along the bottom lets you jump between every image for that object without closing the viewer.
tourGallery.step2Alt: Full-size image viewer for the Eagle Nebula with Fit, 1:1, favorite, share, and download controls, and a filmstrip of other images below
tourGallery.step3Body: Search narrows the grid to one object's frames across every session. Hover a thumbnail to favorite it right from the grid, or click through to see which object and session produced it. Favorites and Processed only combine with search, so you can find a specific final fast even in a large library.
tourGallery.step3Alt: Gallery filtered by search to Eagle Nebula, with a favorite heart icon showing on hover over the first thumbnail
tourGallery.note: Your Gallery automatically updates as you import new frames or upload processed images from any object or session. It's a living collection of your astrophotography achievements.

tourObservations.title: Observations
tourObservations.lead: Every imaging session you've ever logged, browsable by calendar, list, or map.
tourObservations.step1Title: See your imaging activity at a glance
tourObservations.step1Body: The header totals nights out, distinct objects, sessions, and files across your whole history, and a bar chart breaks sessions down by month for the selected year. Below it, the Calendar view lays out every session on the day it happened, with a thumbnail and time for each object. Nights you planned in the Planner show next to what you shot, so you can see where a plan did not turn into pictures. The banner at the top folds to one slim row with the page's key figures.
tourObservations.step1Alt: Observations page showing lifetime totals, a monthly bar chart, and a calendar grid with session thumbnails on each day
tourObservations.step2Title: Switch to a list, or a map of where you've observed
tourObservations.step2Body: The List view is a sortable table of every session by object, catalog id, and date, good for scanning a long history fast. Filter either view down to one telescope with the scope dropdown, or to one rig (an optical setup such as Native or Reducer 0.75x) with the Rig filter. The List view has a Rig column too. Use Share to hand someone a read-only link.
tourObservations.step2Alt: Observations List view showing a sortable table of sessions with Object, Catalog, and Date columns
tourObservations.step3Body: Click any session to open its full detail page: the stacked image, integration time, frames stacked, exposure and filter used, plus panels for the object itself, sky conditions that night, and where you observed from. Its Sub-frames list scores every raw frame (see Frame quality and stacking). Add notes, choose the rig, combine subs, or delete the session from here.
tourObservations.step3Alt: M45 Pleiades observation detail page showing the stacked image, integration stats, and About, Conditions, and Observed from panels
tourObservations.step4Body: The Map view plots every session by location, clustered by how many you logged nearby. If you observe from more than one site, home, a dark-sky trip, a friend's backyard, this is the fastest way to see your history spread across them.
tourObservations.step4Alt: Observations Map view showing session location clusters across the southeastern United States
tourObservations.note: Every observation is permanently linked to its object. Even years later, you'll be able to see exactly what you captured, when, with which equipment, and under what conditions.

tourForecast.title: Forecast
tourForecast.lead: A single 0–100 score for tonight, plus the astronomical facts and weather behind it.
tourForecast.step1Title: Read tonight's score at a glance
tourForecast.step1Body: The ring on the left boils cloud cover, seeing and jet stream, and moon interference down to one 0–100 rating with a plain-language verdict underneath. Dark hours, sunset, sunrise, and the best imaging window sit alongside it, and the ribbon below traces sky quality through the night, worst to best, so you can see exactly when it gets good.
tourForecast.step1Alt: Sky Forecast page showing a 55/100 Good rating, moon phase, dark hours, sunset and sunrise times, best window, and a colored night-quality ribbon
tourForecast.step2Body: Below the ribbon, "The nights ahead" cards give each upcoming night its own score and a cloud-cover trend line, so you can tell at a glance whether tomorrow is worth staying up for or better spent processing what you already have.
tourForecast.step2Alt: Two upcoming-night cards showing a 64 Good score for Thursday and a 94 Excellent score for Friday, each with a cloud cover trend line
tourForecast.step3Body: If you've set up more than one site under Settings → Sky, the location picker in the top right switches the whole forecast between them instantly. Handy for comparing home against a dark-sky spot before deciding where to drive.
tourForecast.step3Alt: Location picker open showing Franklin Tennessee, Nashville - West, and Russia as selectable observing sites
tourForecast.note: Forecast data comes from open-meteo and 7Timer, combined into one score tuned for imaging rather than general weather.

tourPlanner.title: Planner
tourPlanner.lead: Build tonight's schedule target by target, and watch conflicts and free time update as you go.
tourPlanner.step1Title: Add targets to build your schedule
tourPlanner.step1Body: Search or browse the Targets list on the left, each one shows its magnitude, constellation, and when it peaks tonight, and tap + to drop it onto the Night schedule on the right. Nebulis picks a sensible time window automatically; drag a block's handle to nudge it, or use the day picker up top to plan any of the next two weeks. The Order menu above the list sorts targets by Best tonight or Best conditions, and the compass button opens Explore on the night you are planning. A target with time left toward its goals shows it, such as "4h left · Ha".
tourPlanner.step1Alt: Planner page with three targets added to the night schedule, showing scheduled time blocks and remaining free time
tourPlanner.step2Title: See exactly when each target is well placed
tourPlanner.step2Body: Scroll down and the altitude chart plots a curve for every scheduled target across the night, shaded over the span it's actually booked for. It's the fastest way to check a target isn't scheduled while it's still low on the horizon.
tourPlanner.step2Alt: Altitude curve chart showing three scheduled targets with their curves shaded over their booked time windows
tourPlanner.step3Body: If two targets land in the same window, their blocks sit side by side in the schedule instead of stacking, an unmistakable sign you've overcommitted the night. Drag one to a free slot, or remove it with the × on the card.
tourPlanner.step3Alt: Night schedule showing two targets both booked for 22:20 to 23:50, their blocks placed side by side to flag the overlap
tourPlanner.step4Title: Check the moon and darkness for the night
tourPlanner.step4Body: The header sums up the night before you add anything: a Fair/Good/Excellent score, moon phase and illumination with its set time, and how many objects out of your whole catalog are visible tonight. The banner folds to one slim row with the key figures, and Nebulis remembers your choice. Under the banner, the night strip has a legend for its bars, dots and Moon disks. The header also says which kind of filter suits tonight, broadband or narrowband, given the Moon.
tourPlanner.step4Alt: Planner header showing a Fair score, Waxing Gibbous moon at 61% illuminated, and a Plan my night button
tourPlanner.step5Title: Let Plan my night fill the gaps
tourPlanner.step5Body: Plan my night builds a schedule from your targets. It reads the hourly forecast, leaves cloudy slots empty and says which, and puts small targets in the steadiest air. It suggests the filter with the most time left that the Moon allows, and favours objects with time left toward their goals. You can mark any block broadband or narrowband. Objects you can only image in narrowband count as narrowband only when your Gear lists a dual-band, tri-band or narrowband filter. Turn the weather check off in the Plan my night dialog if you want a plan that ignores clouds.
tourPlanner.step5Alt: The Plan my night dialog, with the weather option and the proposed blocks, each with a suggested filter
tourPlanner.step6Title: Compare the plan with what you shot
tourPlanner.step6Body: A scheduled block shows how much was captured, for example 1h 40m / 3h. A block that ended less than a day ago with nothing imported yet shows Awaiting import. If you missed a block, plan it again the next night or mark it skipped.
tourPlanner.step6Alt: Scheduled blocks showing captured time against planned time, and one marked Awaiting import
tourPlanner.rankingIntro: Best tonight means the same thing in the Planner, Explore and Wishlist: how well a target is placed tonight, blended with how rewarding it is to shoot. Placement comes from the factors below, listed from most to least important. Plan my night uses the same ranking.
tourPlanner.rankAltitudeBody: The higher the target climbs, the less atmosphere its light crosses, so it images sharper and cleaner.
tourPlanner.rankHoursBody: Hours the target is above the horizon between the end and start of darkness. Targets up all night score highest.
tourPlanner.rankBrightnessBody: Brighter objects rank higher. Faint ones need more total exposure, and objects with no magnitude on record get a neutral score.
tourPlanner.rankPeakBody: A small bonus for targets that reach their highest point near the middle of the night.
tourPlanner.rankSizeBody: Objects that fill a good part of the frame without overflowing it rank best. Very small or very large ones rank lower, and objects with no size on record get a neutral score.
tourPlanner.moonBody: Each scheduled block is checked against the Moon. The closer the Moon is to full, the farther away a target needs to be: about 25° from a new Moon, about 55° at a quarter Moon and about 85° from a full Moon. A block gets a caution when it is slightly inside that distance and a warning when it is well inside. If the Moon is below the horizon for the whole block, there is no warning. Blocks marked narrowband are judged more leniently: a nebula 40 degrees from a full Moon is not flagged red when it is shot through a narrowband filter.
tourPlanner.note: A well-organized plan means you'll spend less time searching for targets and more time imaging. Use the planner to maximize your productive observing hours.

tourExplore.title: Explore
tourExplore.lead: Find something worth photographing, from your own site and with your own telescope.
tourExplore.step1Body: Explore is in the top menu. Type any name or catalog number (Pelican, M42, Caldwell 14) into the search box, or browse by kind: Galaxies, Emission nebulae, Planetary nebulae, Supernova remnants, Star clusters and Showpieces. Browse tiles work offline. The Download catalog images job also fetches the best objects in each category, so run it once while you have a connection.
tourExplore.step1Alt: The Explore page with a search box and tiles for each kind of object
tourExplore.step2Title: Know before you commit a night
tourExplore.step2Body: Each object says whether you can see it from your site tonight, or in which months if not. It also says whether it fits your telescope's frame, is a tight crop, is tiny, or needs a mosaic. Best tonight is the same score the Planner and Wishlist use.
tourExplore.step2Alt: A category page of object cards, each marked as up tonight or not, and with a note on how it fits the frame
tourExplore.step3Body: Add an object to your wishlist, plan it for tonight, or open Plan a night to pick from the next 30 nights. The Wishlist page's Add target button opens Explore, and Explore and Wishlist cards link back to the Planner. If you don't use Explore, hide its tab under Settings → General → Navigation bar.
tourExplore.step3Alt: An Explore card with the wishlist, Plan tonight and Plan a night buttons
tourExplore.note: Explore judges visibility from the observing site shown in its banner and framing from your telescope's field of view. Set both up under Settings → Sky and Settings → Telescopes first. If you have more than one site, switch between them in the banner.

tourCatalogs.title: Catalogs
tourCatalogs.lead: Track your progress through classic observing programs, and research your next target.
tourCatalogs.step1Title: Pick a catalog to work through
tourCatalogs.step1Body: Catalogs opens on a scoreboard: how many unique objects you've imaged across every catalog combined, then a card for each one, Messier, Caldwell, Herschel 400, Sharpless, with its imaged percentage and a breakdown by galaxies, nebulae, clusters, and other. Open a board to start working through it.
tourCatalogs.step1Alt: Catalogs landing page showing overall progress and catalog cards for Messier, Caldwell, Herschel 400, and Sharpless with imaged percentages
tourCatalogs.step2Title: Browse a catalog and see what you still need
tourCatalogs.step2Body: Inside a board, filter to All, Imaged, or Remaining, search by name or constellation, and the grid marks every object you've already captured with a checkmark and session count. It's the fastest way to see what's left on a list like Messier or Caldwell.
tourCatalogs.step2Alt: Messier catalog board showing progress bars by object type and a grid of objects with checkmarks and session counts on imaged ones
tourCatalogs.step3Title: Look up an object before you shoot it
tourCatalogs.step3Body: Click any entry to open a quick-reference card: type, constellation, magnitude, coordinates, a description with a Wikipedia link, and a bar chart of its maximum altitude for each of the next 12 months so you know which season suits it best.
tourCatalogs.step3Alt: M16 Eagle Nebula quick reference card showing a description, Wikipedia link, and a monthly max-altitude bar chart with Feb through Oct highlighted as the best window
tourCatalogs.step4Title: Jump straight to observing or planning it
tourCatalogs.step4Body: From that same card, View observations takes you to everything you've already captured of it, and Open in Planner drops it onto tonight's schedule. Objects you've already imaged carry their session count right in the grid, so you always know where you stand before you commit a night to it.
tourCatalogs.step4Alt: Catalog grid showing checkmark badges and session counts on imaged objects like Pleiades (17 sessions) and Orion Nebula (13 sessions)
tourCatalogs.step5Title: Count objects that were in your frame
tourCatalogs.step5Body: An object that sat inside the frame of something you imaged counts as imaged too. Imaging M42 also counts M43, and imaging M51 also counts NGC 5195. These tiles show "In M42", and the object card says which object it was imaged with and opens it. How many objects count depends on your telescope's field of view, so a wider scope picks up more. Turn it off under Settings → Library → Credit objects in the same frame.
tourCatalogs.step5Alt: A catalog grid with an In NGC6823 badge on a tile imaged inside another object's frame, among tiles with the Imaged badge
tourCatalogs.step6Title: Hang your own pictures on a wall
tourCatalogs.step6Body: Open My Catalog from a catalog's board to see a wall of your own pictures, one tile for each object you have imaged. Use edit mode to choose which picture each tile shows, then save the wall as a poster.
tourCatalogs.step6Alt: My Catalog wall for Messier, with a picture on each imaged tile and the edit mode controls
tourCatalogs.note: Catalog entries carry distance and angular size where known. To find something new to shoot, use Explore, which also tells you whether an object fits your telescope's field of view.

tourSettings.title: Settings
tourSettings.lead: Configure your app, manage storage, connect devices, and control your Nebulis experience.
tourSettings.step1Body: The search box at the top finds any setting by name and jumps to it. Press / to focus it. The sidebar is grouped under Equipment, System and Advanced, and only the page you are on stays open. Settings → General covers the look and feel of the app: Light, Dark, Space, or Night theme, which menu items show in the top bar (Explore, Wishlist, Calibrations and others can be hidden), measurement units, and Compact page banners, which starts every page with its banner folded.
tourSettings.step1Alt: Settings with the search box at the top, the grouped sidebar, and the General pane showing themes and navigation bar toggles
tourSettings.step2Title: Manage your account and connected devices
tourSettings.step2Body: In Settings → Account, manage users (admin or viewer) and see every phone, tablet, or TV paired to your library. Connect a device to generate a QR code for quick pairing, and revoke access for any device you no longer use.
tourSettings.step2Alt: Settings → Account → Devices, with a Connect a device button and an empty device list
tourSettings.step3Body: Add your smart telescopes, cameras, or network sources. Support includes ZWO SeeStar, ZWO ASIAIR, DWARFLAB Dwarf series, and standard SMB network shares. For each telescope, configure the connection type (Wi-Fi or USB), network settings, and enable/disable to control syncing. Press Find device to discover nearby devices, or enter the connection details yourself. Sync calibration frames, on by default, also copies a SeeStar's darklibrary folder, Dwarf CALI_FRAME and ASIAIR Dark, Flat and Bias, so they show on the Calibrations page. Under Edit you can add your own photo of the telescope. A cut-out on a transparent background looks best.
tourSettings.step3Alt: Telescopes settings showing list of connected devices with connection status
tourSettings.step4Body: Settings → Sky is where the Planner, Forecast and Explore get their facts. Observing sites holds each site's coordinates, timezone and minimum altitude, and you can add photos of the garden, the skyline or the spot you set up from. Catalog data holds the offline catalogs and data sources such as satellite trail tracking.
tourSettings.step4Alt: Settings → Sky, showing an observing site with its name, coordinates, and minimum altitude
tourSettings.step5Body: Check your total library storage usage and see a breakdown by object. Find which objects are using the most disk space. Move your library to a different drive or network location if needed. Manage your backups and set automated backup schedules to protect your imaging data. Cleanup runs Library Health, which now includes a Duplicate session files check. It finds a capture stored twice under one object and deletes the second copy only after the bytes match the first.
tourSettings.step5Alt: Storage settings showing total usage, per-object breakdown, and library location controls
tourSettings.step6Title: Connect other devices and manage pairing
tourSettings.step6Body: Pair your iPad, iPhone, Apple TV, or web browsers to access your library remotely. Generate QR codes for quick pairing, view all connected devices, and revoke access from devices you no longer use. Each device gets its own authentication token for secure access.
tourSettings.step6Alt: Devices settings showing list of paired devices with revoke buttons
tourSettings.step7Body: Access advanced settings like enabling night mode (red-tinted interface for dark adaptation), adjusting satellite trail detection sensitivity, clearing cached data, resetting the app, and viewing logs. Export your data or import previously backed up libraries.
tourSettings.step7Alt: Advanced settings showing theme options, data management, and expert controls
tourSettings.step8Body: Settings → Library holds the options behind several 2.2 features: the default Object pages layout (Combined or Classic), Analyze frames after import, which measures new nights in the background, plate solving of stacked pictures for Annotate, Credit objects in the same frame, and Filter aliases, which merge filter names that differ between telescopes (Ha, H-alpha and H).
tourSettings.step8Alt: Settings → Library, showing the Object pages choice, the frame analysis and plate solving switches, and Filter aliases
tourSettings.step9Title: Send alerts to your phone or chat
tourSettings.step9Body: Settings → Alerts sends a message to an ntfy topic, a Discord or Slack channel, or any webhook. See Alerts for the steps.
tourSettings.step9Alt: Settings → Alerts, listing channels with the events each one receives
tourSettings.note: Settings is where you can fine-tune Nebulis to match your exact workflow. Most settings take effect immediately, though some (like telescope connections) may require a resync.

frames.title: Frame quality and stacking
frames.lead: See which raw frames are worth keeping, then hand the best ones to PixInsight or Siril with the right calibration frames.
frames.step1Body: Open an observation page and look at its Sub-frames list. Opening a night measures it in the background and keeps the results. Every frame gets a score from 0 to 100 and a Good, Fair or Bad grade against the rest of its night, with flags for clouds, star trails, soft stars, satellite or plane streaks, no stars and noise. To measure new nights as soon as they import, turn on Analyze frames after import under Settings → Library.
frames.step1Alt: A night's Sub-frames list with a score, grade and flags for each raw frame
frames.step2Body: Sort any column. The strip above the list shows the whole night and names the longest gap. Turn on Flagged only to hide the good frames, and rest on a row for a larger preview with every reason in words.
frames.step2Alt: The night strip above the Sub-frames list, with a preview open on a flagged frame
frames.step3Body: Mark a frame Keep, Reject, or back to following its grade. In the picture viewer, press K to keep and X to reject. Select bad frames and discard them to free space. A frame in a linked folder asks first. You can also export a night's numbers as a CSV with an accepted column, for PixInsight or Siril scripts.
frames.step3Alt: The Sub-frames list with several frames selected and the Discard button showing
frames.step4Body: On an object page, Analyze Frames opens the same review with a night picker, so you can check a night without opening its observation. Administrators can run it.
frames.step4Alt: The Analyze Frames dialog with a night picker and the frame list
frames.step5Body: Open the object's ... menu and choose Export for stacking. Pick the nights you want, and Nebulis builds a ZIP of the kept lights. It adds the matching darks, flats, flat darks and bias from your Calibration Library, laid out for PixInsight WBPP or Siril, and lists what is missing before you download. Combine subs can leave out rejected and bad frames as well.
frames.step5Alt: The Export for stacking dialog, with nights chosen, the matching calibration frames and a list of what is missing
frames.note: Frame scores are measured against the rest of the same night, so a Bad frame is one that is poor for that night, not one that fails a fixed standard.

integration.title: Integration and rigs
integration.lead: Know how much time each object has, through which filter, and on which optical setup.
integration.step1Body: The object page's Integration card shows the time shot through each filter, a goal you can set per filter, and what is left. Library, Wishlist and Planner cards show it too, as "4h left · Ha".
integration.step1Alt: The Integration card with a bar and a goal for each filter
integration.step2Body: Two telescopes can call the same filter by different names. Merge them under Settings → Library → Filter aliases, for example Ha, H-alpha and H, so the time adds up in one bar.
integration.step2Alt: Filter aliases in Settings → Library, with Ha, H-alpha and H merged
integration.step3Title: Know which rig took each night
integration.step3Body: Each night is tied to one of its telescope's optical configurations, such as Native or Reducer 0.75x. The rig is the one you choose on the observation page. Failing that, Nebulis reads the focal length from the pictures' headers, then falls back to the telescope's only configuration. A folder import has an Optical train choice, so you can set it as you import.
integration.step3Alt: An observation page with the rig picker set to Reducer 0.75x
integration.step4Body: The object page can group nights by rig. The Observations list has a Rig column and a Rig filter.
integration.step4Alt: An object page with nights grouped by rig

annotate.title: Annotate
annotate.lead: Draw rings and names over the objects in a picture, each with a details card.
annotate.step1Title: Open a picture and tap the target
annotate.step1Body: Open a stacked picture in the viewer and tap the target button. Nebulis draws a ring and a name over each object in it. Tap a ring for its details card.
annotate.step1Alt: The image viewer with rings and names drawn over objects in a stacked picture, and a details card open
annotate.step2Title: Let plate solving run in the background
annotate.step2Body: Stacked pictures are plate solved in the background, after each sync and every ten minutes while the library is idle, so the rings are ready when you open a picture. The first time, Nebulis downloads the free ASTAP plate solver (about 100 MB). Pictures that can't be solved are remembered and left alone. To turn it off, go to Settings → Library.
annotate.step2Alt: The plate solving switch in Settings → Library
annotate.step3Title: Download or share with the rings
annotate.step3Body: With the rings showing, Download and Share ask whether to keep the original or save a JPEG with the rings drawn in.
annotate.step3Alt: The Download dialog asking whether to keep the original or save a JPEG with the rings
annotate.note: Annotate is in the web app now. It comes to the iPhone, iPad and Android apps in their 2.1.0 release.

alerts.title: Alerts
alerts.lead: Get a message when a clear night is coming, an import finishes, or an update is available.
alerts.step1Body: Open Settings → Alerts and add a channel: an ntfy topic, a Discord or Slack channel, or any webhook such as Home Assistant or n8n. With ntfy, install the free ntfy app, subscribe to a topic, and paste the topic URL here. Pick a name that is hard to guess. Webhooks can be signed, and you can send a test message to any channel.
alerts.step1Alt: Settings → Alerts, with a channel list and the Add channel form
alerts.step2Body: Pick events for each channel: a clear night is coming, an import finishes or fails, or an update is available. Channels can be paused. The clear-night check runs once each evening, at a time you choose. Messages come in English, French, German, Spanish and Dutch.
alerts.step2Alt: A channel's event switches and the clear-night time
alerts.step3Body: iPhone push needs the iPhone app's 2.1.0 release, which is coming soon. It goes through a small Nebulis relay that stores nothing. Turn on Alerts from this server, then pick what each phone gets under Settings → Alerts → iPhones. Each iPhone can add a Tonight's plan line or a Dew risk warning to its alert.
alerts.step3Alt: The iPhones list in Settings → Alerts, with the extra lines each phone can add

telescopes.title: Adding a telescope or source
telescopes.lead: Nebulis reads files over Wi-Fi or USB, and it can also read a plain folder shared on your network.
telescopes.seestarTerm: ZWO SeeStar S30, S30 Pro, S50, and S50 Pro
telescopes.seestarDef: Wi-Fi over SMB, or USB when the storage is plugged in directly.
telescopes.smbDef: A NAS, PC, or another camera that follows the <1>custom SMB folder layout</1>.
telescopes.step1Title: Go to Settings → Telescopes → Add smart telescope.
telescopes.step2Body: The share name, username, and defaults fill in automatically.
telescopes.step3Title: Choose how to connect, then Test Connection.
telescopes.step3Body: Press Find device to look for SeeStar, ASIAIR and Dwarf devices on your network. Pick one and Nebulis fills in its address and telescope type. Leave Sync calibration frames on, its default, to also copy a SeeStar's darklibrary folder, Dwarf CALI_FRAME and ASIAIR Dark, Flat and Bias. They show on the Calibrations page.
telescopes.note: You can add more than one telescope. Each imports on its own, and the icon in the top bar shows how many are online.
telescopes.altAddSmartTelescope: The Add Smart Telescope dialog with the Telescope Type dropdown set to ZWO SeeStar S50

customSmb.title: Custom SMB sources
customSmb.lead: A NAS, a PC share, or any camera works as a source as long as its files are organized the way Nebulis expects.
customSmb.introBefore: Add it under Settings → Telescopes → Add smart telescope, with the telescope type set to
customSmb.introAfter: Then lay out the share root like this:
customSmb.folderTree:
<share root>/
└── M31/                       one folder per object: a catalog id (M31, NGC1788) or a common name
    ├── 2026-04-26_2030/       session folder, local time: <YYYY-MM-DD>_<HHMM>
    │   ├── lights/            required: at least one stacked or single-shot final
    │   │   ├── M31_stacked.fit
    │   │   └── M31_stacked.jpg
    │   ├── subframes/         optional: individual sub-frames
    │   │   ├── M31_001.fit
    │   │   └── M31_002.fit
    │   └── meta.json          optional: exposureSec, gain, filter, frameCount, integrationSec
    └── 2026-05-03_2115/
        └── lights/...
customSmb.objectFolderDef: Its name is the catalog id or common name Nebulis will file everything under. A recognized catalog id resolves to better metadata than a plain common name.
customSmb.sessionFolderDef: Must match YYYY-MM-DD_HHMM exactly, in local time. The date drives the calendar view; the time keeps two sessions on the same night apart.
customSmb.lightsDef: Required. At least one finished image, FITS master, or single-shot capture. A session folder with no files here is skipped entirely, so a half-finished copy never creates an empty object.
customSmb.subframesDef: Optional. Individual sub-frames for quality scoring and per-frame review. Only pulled in when "Include subframes" is turned on for this source, same as any other telescope.
customSmb.metaJsonDef: Optional. A small JSON file with whatever you know: exposureSec, gain, filter, frameCount, integrationSec. Leave out anything you don't have.
customSmb.filenamesDef: Not parsed at all. Nebulis decides what a file is by which folder it sits in, not by what it's called, so anything with a supported extension in lights/ or subframes/ is picked up.
customSmb.note: Already have files sitting directly inside the object folder with no session subfolders? That still works exactly as before, everything lands in one flat folder for that object. The session-folder layout above is only needed when you want each night kept separate, with sub-frames and metadata alongside it.

importing.title: Importing and syncing images
importing.lead: Importing copies new files from your telescope into the library. Files you have already imported are skipped, so re-running is safe.
importing.bullet1: Sync now: click the telescope icon in the top bar and pick Sync, or use the refresh button on a telescope in Settings. The icon also shows how many telescopes are currently online.
importing.bullet2: Auto-import: turn it on for a telescope in Settings → Telescopes, and Nebulis pulls new captures on a schedule with no clicking needed.
importing.bullet3: First import: the first run copies everything, so give it a few minutes. Later runs only move new files.
importing.bullet4: Folder imports: a folder import shows Finishing once every file is copied, while thumbnails are built. It has an Optical train choice that ties the night to one of the telescope's configurations, such as Native or Reducer 0.75x.
importing.bullet5: Dark library: a SeeStar's darklibrary folder is copied on every sync. If the telescope rebuilds it, the new files replace the copies and the old ones go to a hidden folder.
importing.altSyncDropdown: The telescope pill in the top bar, open to show each telescope with a Sync button and a Sync all option
importing.altBackupStatus: The Backup Status page, showing per-telescope sync state and a history of past syncs
importing.note: Watch progress on the Backup page. It keeps a row for every import with how many files moved, how long it took, and any errors.

uploading.title: Uploading images
uploading.lead: Not everything has to come straight from a telescope. You can bring in files you already have, or log a session by hand.
uploading.bullet1: Upload files: Library → Add → Upload Files. Drag in a folder from your computer, or pick a folder already on the server. You review each object before anything is committed.
uploading.bullet2: Add a processed image: open a session and upload your finished JPG, PNG, or TIFF. It becomes the card thumbnail and shows in the slideshow.
uploading.bullet3: Log an observation: Library → Add → New Observation. Record a session manually with an optional image and notes.
uploading.altUploadFiles: The Import to Library dialog, with a drop zone for a folder and options for subframes and archiving everything
uploading.altNewObservation: The Log Observation dialog, with fields for object, date, image, telescope, and notes

manualImport.title: Manual imports from a folder
manualImport.lead: Point Nebulis at a folder that's already sitting somewhere, either on the computer running Nebulis or on a network share, instead of dragging files through the browser.
manualImport.step1Body: The same dialog used for a browser upload has a second path down at the bottom for files that are already somewhere Nebulis can reach.
manualImport.step1Alt: The Import to Library dialog's drop zone, with a link below it reading 'Files already on the computer running Nebulis? Import in place, no upload.'
manualImport.step2Title: Click "Files already on the computer running Nebulis?"
manualImport.step2Body: This switches to a server-side folder browser: pick a drive Nebulis can see, or type a path directly. Nothing uploads. The server reads the folder where it already sits, so even a huge backup imports in seconds instead of streaming through your browser.
manualImport.step2Alt: The server-side folder picker, listing detected drives and an 'Or enter a path' field with a placeholder showing a UNC path and a drive letter path
manualImport.step3Title: For a NAS or network folder, type its UNC path.
manualImport.step3Body: A network share never shows up in the drive list above, and a mapped drive letter (like <1>Z:</1>) won't work either. Both only exist inside your own sign-in session, and Nebulis runs as a background service that doesn't share it. Type or paste the share's full UNC path instead, for example <3>\\NAS-OBSERVATORY\Astrophotography</3>, and Nebulis browses it the same way as a local drive.
manualImport.step3Alt: The folder picker with a UNC path opened, showing its subfolders SeeStar S50, Dwarf 3, and _archive
manualImport.step3Caption: Upload Files → Import in place → UNC path
manualImport.step4Body: Same review step as any other import: Nebulis shows every object, session, and file it found before anything is committed, so nothing lands in the library unreviewed.
manualImport.note: If typing the UNC path fails with a permission or "cannot read that folder" error, the share itself is reachable but Nebulis isn't allowed onto it yet. See below.

giveAccess.title: Give Nebulis access to that network share
giveAccess.lead: A UNC path only resolves if whatever is running Nebulis is already allowed onto the share, the same way a person would need to be. Nebulis itself has no login prompt for this: it inherits access from the account its background process runs as, so that account is what needs to be squared away with the NAS or PC sharing the folder.
giveAccess.note: A share configured for guest or anonymous access needs none of this: it already works no matter which account Nebulis runs as. This is only for a share that asks for a username and password.

linkedFolders.title: Linked folders
linkedFolders.lead: Already have a folder of captures on a drive? Link it and Nebulis shows its objects in your library without copying a single file.
linkedFolders.step1Title: Open Library → Add → Upload Files and choose Link Data.
linkedFolders.step1Body: Link Data is for files that are already on the computer running Nebulis. Nebulis reads them where they are and copies nothing. If your files are on another computer, or you want Nebulis to keep its own copy, choose Upload Data instead.
linkedFolders.step1Alt: The Import to Library dialog with two choices, Link Data and Upload Data
linkedFolders.step2Body: Choose a drive from the list, or type a path, then open subfolders until the folder you want is shown. You can link the top folder of a whole collection. Nebulis works out which object each file belongs to from the folder and file names beneath it, so you don't have to link one object at a time.
linkedFolders.step2Alt: The Link a folder dialog, showing the drive list, a path field, and the subfolders of the chosen folder
linkedFolders.step3Body: Include subframes adds the individual raw exposures. It is the only option in this step that applies to a link. The others are for copying and are ignored.
linkedFolders.step4Body: Each object is listed with its catalog match, its nights, and how many files belong to it. Uncheck an object to leave it out, and use Change object when a match is wrong. Give the link a name so you can find it in Settings later. Folders that don't say which object they hold are listed separately, and you can assign them to an object or ignore them. Nothing is linked until you continue.
linkedFolders.step4Alt: The review step, showing the label field and a list of objects with catalog matches, nights, and file counts
linkedFolders.step5Title: Choose how the folder stays up to date, then link it.
linkedFolders.step5Body: One-time indexes what is in the folder now. Files you add later appear when you press Rescan in Settings. Ongoing has Nebulis check the folder by itself, every hour, 6 hours, day, or week, and pick up new, changed, and removed files.
linkedFolders.step5Alt: The choice between One-time and Ongoing, with Ongoing selected
linkedFolders.step5Caption: Link Data → Keep up to date
linkedFolders.note: Nebulis never moves or renames anything in a linked folder, and it deletes nothing unless you ask. Deleting an image removes the original from your disk once you confirm, because Nebulis has no other copy. Deleting an object or an observation only removes it from Nebulis, unless you also check the option to delete its original files.

linkedFoldersManage.title: Managing linked folders
linkedFoldersManage.lead: Every linked folder is listed under Settings → Storage → Linked folders, with its object and file counts and when it was last scanned.
linkedFoldersManage.rescanDesc: Compares the folder with what Nebulis has indexed. New files are added, changed files are updated, and a summary shows when it finishes.
linkedFoldersManage.editDesc: Rename the link, or change how often Nebulis checks the folder.
linkedFoldersManage.unlinkDesc: Removes the folder from Nebulis. Its objects leave your library unless they have notes, favorites, or files from another source. Your files on disk are not touched.
linkedFoldersManage.offlineDesc: If the drive or share can't be reached, the folder is marked as unreachable and nothing changes. Reconnect it and rescan.
linkedFoldersManage.missingDesc: A file that has gone missing stays in the index until a second scan confirms it is gone, so a scan taken while a folder is half-mounted doesn't empty your library.
linkedFoldersManage.settingsAlt: Settings, Storage, Linked folders, listing two linked folders with Rescan, Edit, and Unlink buttons
linkedFoldersManage.note: Linked files are not included when you archive to an external disk. Archiving copies only the files in the Nebulis library itself.

archive.title: Archive to an external disk
archive.lead: Copy your library to a disk you can unplug, so your captures survive if the computer or drive they live on fails. Archiving is off until you turn it on, and nothing is copied or deleted before the last setup step.
archive.step1Title: Open Settings → Storage → Archive and choose the disk.
archive.step1Body: Select Set up archive, then Choose folder. Pick a drive, or use the Network share tab for a NAS, and choose or create a folder on it. Choosing a folder doesn't write anything to the disk. Nebulis claims the folder as your archive only when you turn the archive on, and it remembers the disk, so a different disk mounted at the same path is never mistaken for it.
archive.step1Alt: The Choose the archive destination dialog, listing drives with the Archive drive selected
archive.step2Body: Include subframes copies the individual raw exposures. They are most of the size and most of the value of a backup, so leave this on unless space is tight. Wait before archiving keeps new captures on this computer until they reach the age you set, so nights you are still processing are not copied yet.
archive.step2Alt: The What to copy step, with an Include subframes switch and a Wait before archiving field
archive.step3Body: Run it by hand, every day at a set time, every few hours, or on a custom cron schedule. Times use the timezone of your observing site. Each run copies what is new and skips what is already on the disk. A custom schedule runs at its exact minute and does not catch up if Nebulis was closed then.
archive.step3Alt: The Schedule step, with Manual only, Every day, Every few hours, and Custom, and a time of day
archive.step4Body: Both cleanup options are off by default, and they are the only settings that delete anything. Prune the archive automatically removes old files from the archive disk after the number of days you set, either whole objects or subframes only, and only files your library still has. Remove local subframes after archiving frees space on this computer by deleting subframes once their archived copy is verified by size and checksum.
archive.step4Alt: The Cleanup step, with switches for pruning the archive and removing local subframes, both off
archive.step5Body: The last step sums up what the archive will do in plain sentences. Check that the disk is the one you expect, then select Turn on archive.
archive.note: Removing local subframes is permanent. If the archive disk is lost afterward, those frames are gone, so leave it off until you trust the archive. Keep the archive on a different disk from your library too. An archive on the same disk won't survive that disk failing, and Nebulis warns you if they match.

archiveManage.title: Running and managing the archive
archiveManage.lead: Once the archive is on, Settings → Storage → Archive shows the disk, whether it is your archive disk, and the result of the last run.
archiveManage.runDesc: Starts a run right away. Files already on the disk are skipped, so runs after the first are quick.
archiveManage.browseDesc: Shows what is on the disk and lets you restore files from it. See the next section.
archiveManage.turnOffDesc: Stops all copying and deleting. Your settings are kept, so you can turn the archive back on later.
archiveManage.editDesc: Disk, What to copy, Schedule, and Cleanup each open on their own and save separately.
archiveManage.overviewAlt: The archive overview, showing the disk, Archive now, Browse archive, and Turn off buttons, and the four settings groups

archiveRestore.title: Restoring from the archive
archiveRestore.lead: Browsing the archive only reads the disk. Nothing changes in your library until you choose files to restore.
archiveRestore.step1Body: Each object on the disk is listed with its file and subframe counts, and how many of its files are missing from this computer.
archiveRestore.step1Alt: The Archive disk dialog, listing three objects with file counts and how many are missing locally
archiveRestore.step2Title: Open an object and check the files you want.
archiveRestore.step2Body: Each file shows whether it is present or missing locally. Check the ones to bring back and select Restore.
archiveRestore.step2Alt: The file list for one object, with two subframes checked
archiveRestore.step3Body: If a file on the disk differs from the copy already in your library, Nebulis lists those files and asks before replacing them. Restored files come back with their size, capture date, and telescope. A night you moved to another date by hand goes back to the date in the file name.

serviceAccountTabs.winIntro: Nebulis installs as a Windows service, which by default runs as <1>Local System</1>, a machine identity with no credentials on your NAS or PC. Give the service an account the share already trusts:
serviceAccountTabs.winStep1Body: Press <1>Win + R</1>, type <3>services.msc</3>, and press Enter.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep2Title: Find Nebulis, then open its Log On tab.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep2Body: Right-click <1>Nebulis</1> in the list → Properties → the <3>Log On</3> tab.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep3Title: Switch to "This account" and enter its credentials.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep3Body: Use an account the share already grants access to: a local account as <1>.\username</1>, or a domain account as <3>DOMAIN\username</3>. Enter its password, click OK, and Windows grants that account the "Log on as a service" right automatically.
serviceAccountTabs.winStep4Body: Right-click Nebulis → Restart, or from an elevated prompt: <1>net stop Nebulis && net start Nebulis</1>.
serviceAccountTabs.winFooter: Re-registered the service by hand with <1>install-service.bat</1> instead of the installer? Set the account from the command line first: <3>nssm.exe set Nebulis ObjectName ".\username" "password"</3>, then restart it the same way.
serviceAccountTabs.macIntro: The Mac build has no separate service account: Nebulis runs as a LaunchAgent inside whichever macOS user is currently logged in, so it already has that user's access. The fix here is making sure that account can reach the share, not swapping the account Nebulis uses.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep1Title: Connect to the share once from Finder.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep1Body: Press <1>Cmd + K</1> (Finder → Go → Connect to Server), enter <3>smb://host/share</3>, and sign in with the credentials the folder needs. Turn on <5>Remember this password in my keychain</5> so it reconnects on its own later.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep2Title: Use the /Volumes path, not the smb:// address.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep2Body: Once mounted it appears under <1>/Volumes/</1>, e.g. <3>/Volumes/Astrophotography</3>. That's the path to type into Nebulis's folder picker.
serviceAccountTabs.macStep3Title: Logged in as a different user than the share credentials belong to?
serviceAccountTabs.macStep3Body: Log in as (or fast-user-switch to) the macOS account that owns those credentials before opening Nebulis, since the LaunchAgent runs inside whichever account is signed in at the time.

mobileDevices.title: Mobile devices
mobileDevices.lead: iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, and Android apps that read the same library over your local network. No cloud, no subscription, no separate account to manage.
mobileDevices.step1Title: Download the app for your device
mobileDevices.step1Body: iPhone, iPad, and Apple TV share one app on the App Store; Android has its own on Google Play. Each is a one-time $4.99 purchase, while the Nebulis server itself stays free. Both connect to this same server, so anything you capture, star, or process on the web shows up there too.
mobileDevices.step1Alt: The Mobile menu open in the top bar, showing Scan QR code, Enter code, and download links for iPhone/iPad/Apple TV and Android
mobileDevices.step2Title: Connect a phone or tablet with a QR code
mobileDevices.step2Body: Click the <1>Mobile</1> button in the top bar and choose <3>Scan QR code</3>. Open Nebulis on your phone, tap Scan QR, and point it at the code on screen. It connects and signs you in together, no typing an IP address. The code refreshes itself and expires after ten minutes if it isn't used.
mobileDevices.step2Alt: The Connect a device dialog with a QR code to scan from the Nebulis phone app, plus a manual address fallback
mobileDevices.step3Title: Link an Apple TV with a short code
mobileDevices.step3Body: A TV has no camera, so pairing works the other way around: open Nebulis on the Apple TV and it displays a four-character code. Back on the web, click <1>Mobile</1> → <3>Enter code</3>, type what's on screen, and confirm the TV name that comes up.
mobileDevices.step3Alt: The Link an Apple TV dialog with a four-character code input field
mobileDevices.step4Body: Every phone, tablet, and TV you've linked shows up under Settings → Account → Devices. Each one carries its own sign-in token, so revoking a device here cuts its access immediately without touching anyone else's.
mobileDevices.step4Alt: Settings → Account → Devices, with a Connect a device button and an empty device list
mobileDevices.note: Annotate, iPhone push alerts and photos of your observing sites arrive in the iPhone and iPad app's 2.1.0 release, and Annotate in the Android app's too.

pixinsight.title: PixInsight integration
pixinsight.lead: Browse your library from inside PixInsight, download a night's sub-frames, find matching calibration frames, and back up your processing projects. Turn it on first in Settings → Integrations.
pixinsight.step1Body: Open Settings → Integrations, switch on PixInsight integration and save. Nebulis then serves the connector from its own address.
pixinsight.step2Title: Add the Nebulis repository in PixInsight
pixinsight.step2Body: In PixInsight choose Resources → Updates → Manage Repositories → Add and paste the repository URL shown under the switch (keep the trailing slash). Then run Resources → Updates → Check for Updates, apply the update and restart PixInsight. After a Nebulis upgrade, the same check keeps the connector current.
pixinsight.step3Body: Open Settings → API keys, create a key named for your computer and copy it. It is shown only once. The key has your access: an admin key can upload project files, a viewer key can only browse and download.
pixinsight.step4Body: In PixInsight open Script → Nebulis → Nebulis Connector, click Settings, enter this server's address and the key, and test the connection. Library & Download fetches a night's sub-frames, Calibration Library finds matching darks, flats and bias, and Project Sync stores process icons and project files with the object under Project archives.
pixinsight.troubleshooting: Nothing at the repository URL means the feature is switched off. Uploading project files needs the curl command, which Windows 10 and later, macOS and most Linux systems include.

troubleshooting.title: Troubleshooting
troubleshooting.lead: The problems people actually run into.
troubleshooting.bullet1: The telescope will not connect: check both are on the same Wi-Fi, try the IP instead of the hostname, and check the share name. Use Test connection in the telescope editor to see the exact error.
troubleshooting.bullet2: An import is stuck or slow: weak Wi-Fi and large FITS files are the usual causes. Cancel and retry; it resumes where it stopped.
troubleshooting.bullet3: A new session is not showing up: clear filters in the Library, check the import log on the Backup page, then re-run the import.
troubleshooting.bullet4: The Planner is empty: almost always the location is unset or the minimum altitude is too high. Check Settings → Sky and lower it.
troubleshooting.bullet5: The library says it is unavailable: check the drive it is stored on is connected, or that the network share is reachable.

mobileAppsPromo.title: Nebulis Mobile Apps
mobileAppsPromo.heading: Nebulis on Mobile
mobileAppsPromo.subtitle: Take your library anywhere
mobileAppsPromo.body1: Thank you for using Nebulis. I believe your images and data belong to you, which is why I built this as a free, secure, self-hosted solution. Your library stays on your hardware, no accounts, no subscriptions, and no data leaving your network.
mobileAppsPromo.body2: The mobile apps let you browse your library on the go, or pull it up on your TV (Apple TV). I charge a small one-time fee ($4.99) to help cover ongoing development costs on those platforms.

whatsNewV20.title: What's new in Nebulis 2.0
whatsNewV20.subtitle: A full UI redesign, a night-first Planner and Sky Forecast, and a guided tour to get new users started.

planner.title: Planner, redesigned around picking a night
planner.lead: See two weeks at a glance.
planner.description: A two-week strip shows each night's forecast rating, Moon phase, and whether you already have a plan. The schedule reads the weather forecast hour by hour, with a twilight gradient and a line marking the current time.

forecast.title: Sky Forecast, redesigned around tonight
forecast.description: A single rating, the Moon at its real phase, and a night ribbon covering twilight, clouds, Moon-up hours, and visibility on one timeline, plus a best-window readout for the nights ahead.

catalogs.title: Sharpless joins the catalogs
catalogs.lead: A new catalog to work through.
catalogs.description: The Sharpless catalog of emission nebulae is now part of the set, alongside Messier, Caldwell, and Herschel 400. Each has a progress board showing what you've captured and what's still up, and search matches any of an object's catalog names.

observations.title: Observations, redesigned
observations.description: See your observations as a month-by-month chart, on a map, or as a list. The page opens on your nights out and your objects, and the calendar lands on your most recent night with each day showing its photo.

guidedTour.title: Guided Tour
guidedTour.description: A guided tour launches automatically on a new install and walks you through the app. Restart it anytime from Help -> Start the Guided Tour.

helpPage.title: New Help page
helpPage.description: Screenshots and walkthroughs for importing, syncing, planning, and more, all in one place.

systemLog.title: System Log for admins
systemLog.description: A searchable history of sign-ins, user changes, telescope and device changes, syncs, and settings changes. Settings -> System Log.

backupStatus.title: Backup Status, redesigned
backupStatus.description: A live progress banner shows transfer rate and time left while syncing, and a backup history records every past sync. Each telescope card shows when it last synced, and a failed sync gets its own panel with the full error text.

databaseBackup.title: Automatic database backups
databaseBackup.description: Nebulis snapshots its database automatically just before it applies a new version, so you can return to an earlier release without losing data. Make one yourself, or manage the rest, at Settings -> Storage -> Backups.

whatsNewV22.title: What's new in Nebulis 2.2
whatsNewV22.subtitle: Explore what to shoot next, name every object in a picture, and see which frames are worth stacking.

explore.title: Explore
explore.description: Search any name or catalog number, or browse by kind. Every object says whether you can see it from your site and whether it fits your telescope's frame. Add it to the wishlist or plan it for any of the next 30 nights.

annotate.title: Annotate
annotate.description: Tap the target button in the viewer to draw rings and names over the objects in a frame. New stacks are plate solved in the background, so the rings are ready when you open them.

frameQuality.title: Frame quality
frameQuality.lead: See which frames are worth keeping.
frameQuality.description: Every raw frame gets a score and flags for clouds, star trails, soft stars and satellite streaks. Sort the list, rest on a row for a preview, keep or reject frames, and export the numbers as a CSV.

myCatalog.title: My Catalog
myCatalog.lead: A wall of your own pictures.
myCatalog.description: Each catalog gets a wall of the pictures you have taken. Choose what each tile shows, then save the wall as a poster.

myMedia.title: Combined object page
myMedia.lead: Every picture of an object, on one page.
myMedia.description: Pictures, sub-frames, nights and project files on one page, in tabs, with no digging through observations.

integration.title: Integration by filter
integration.lead: Know what is left to shoot.
integration.description: See the time shot through each filter, set a goal for each one, and watch the bar fill. Library, Wishlist and Planner cards show what is left, like "4h left · Ha".

planMyNight.title: Smarter Plan My Night
planMyNight.description: Plan My Night reads the hourly forecast and skips cloudy hours, suggests a filter for each block, and favours objects with time left toward their goals.

mosaic.title: Mosaic layout
mosaic.description: Switch the Library or the Gallery to a mosaic, where each tile is sized by how much you have done with that object.

exportStacking.title: Export for stacking
exportStacking.description: Build a ZIP of your kept lights with the matching darks, flats and bias from your Calibration Library. It shows what is missing before you download.

connectionMethodTabs.wifiBody: A SeeStar is usually <1>seestar.local</1> or the IP from its app. A Dwarf defaults to <3>192.168.88.1</3> only when it broadcasts its own access point; joined to your home Wi-Fi it takes whatever address your router assigns. A green result means you are ready to import.

connectionMethodTabs.usbBody: Plug the telescope's storage into this computer and tap the refresh icon to detect it, or type the path yourself if you already know it.

connectionMethodTabs.networkBody: For a NAS, a PC share, or another camera, pick <1>Other (custom SMB share)</1> as the telescope type, then enter the host and the share name.
